idiom_name: PORO DAO over Sequel datasets (with ActiveRecord models as the alternative)
implementation_notes: Ruby's data access is dominated by two libraries: Sequel, whose datasets are frozen value objects that build SQL functionally (DB[:customer].where(id: id).first touches the database only when a returning method is called), and ActiveRecord, whose models mix the row with domain logic and finders. A DAO is therefore a plain Ruby object holding an injected database handle, executing through one of those libraries and returning domain objects or hashes, while the library supplies pooling, SQL generation and transactions. What replaces the classic interface-per-store structure is the injected handle plus duck typing; the explicit form still earns its keep when one aggregate is served by two stores, because then the DAO object is the only name business code mentions.
pitfalls: Sequel datasets are lazy and immutable: returning one from the DAO hands callers the query builder and moves the execution point out of the boundary, so always materialise (first/all/insert/update).
ActiveRecord-style models carry their own persistence and query interface; using them as the DAO's return type gives business code finders and relations again, which is the coupling the DAO removed.

Database handles are bound to a connection or pool: sharing one across threads (Puma, Thread.new) without the library's pool corrupts connections, and Sequel's dataset methods are thread-safe only on top of a proper pool.
